1:
Chrysostom begins from the office, calling the dignity of an apostle great and admirable and noticing that Paul constantly sets out the grounds of it, not as a man taking honour to himself but as one entrusted with it and under a necessity of saying so. Calvin asks the sharper question of why the claim is made at all in a private letter, since had he written to Timothy alone there would have been no need to assert the designation and maintain it as he does, Timothy having no doubt of it; the title is therefore for other eyes. Gill answers in the same way, that the office is named less for Timothy's sake than for those to whom what follows must come with weight and authority. Robertson finds the force in the preposition, since the idiom used means by way of command, so that Paul is an apostle under orders. Henry counts the credentials and finds them unquestionable, a commandment as well as a commission, and from Jesus Christ as well as from God our Saviour. Wesley draws the manner from it, that familiarity is to be set aside where the things of God are concerned.

Clarke works on the word apostle itself, which literally means only a person sent from one to another and implies no dignity in the sender's messenger or importance in the message; but in the New Testament it belongs to men sent expressly from God with the message of salvation, and so becomes the highest character any human being can bear. On the title given to the Father, Barnes observes that Saviour applies as properly to God as to the Lord Jesus, since God is the great author of salvation, and Wesley says he is so styled elsewhere as the grand orderer of the whole scheme. Clarke takes the last title as the summary of the rest: without Jesus the world was hopeless, and he is called our hope exactly as he is called our life, our peace and our righteousness, because from him all of these proceed. Ellicott hears something more personal in it, a guiding star burning before an old man in danger, and reads the letter as written with a double purpose, an affectionate reminder from Paul the Aged to his disciple to stand fast amid the perils of his position.

Whether Paul was Timothy's spiritual father in fact is a real disagreement. Barnes states it plainly, that Timothy was converted to the faith by his instrumentality, and that Paul, having no children of his own, adopted him as a son and always treated him so. Gill denies the premise: Timothy was already a converted disciple, well reported of by the brethren, when Paul first met him, so the apostle was not properly the instrument of his conversion, and the name of son must come either from the young man's age, or from affection, or rather from his having been more largely instructed by Paul afterwards. Clarke supplies a rabbinic maxim that would settle it either way, that he who teaches the law to his neighbour's son is reckoned by Scripture to have begotten him, the proof being that Aaron begot his sons while Moses instructed them and they are named after Moses; and he allows besides that the Greek may simply mean beloved son. Robertson glosses the same word as legitimate rather than spurious. Ellicott and Wesley both notice the added mercy in the greeting, which Ellicott traces to an old man's deepening tenderness.
3:
Barnes reads the opening sentence as evidence of the circumstances behind it, that Paul and Timothy had been working together at Ephesus and that Paul was compelled to leave before finishing what he meant to do, so that the charge left behind was not a single order he could have given himself before departing but a standing commission. Clarke supplies the same reconstruction with a motive attached, that a bad seed had been sown in the church and Paul, obliged to go into Macedonia, wanted a man on whose prudence and soundness he could depend to stay and prevent a pernicious doctrine from spreading. Ellicott dates the parting after the first Roman imprisonment and beyond the period covered by the Acts, and attends to what the letter does not say: the false teachers are not named, and though there may be a ring of contempt in the word some, it seems likelier that the names were left out because the letter was meant to be a public document, the chief officer at Ephesus knowing perfectly well who was intended. Robertson notes that the vagueness is deliberate, since Paul names names readily enough at the end of the chapter.

The fables are agreed to be Jewish, and the commentators compete in describing them. Barnes traces the word from speech to fiction and to mystic discourse, allows that such things abounded among Greeks as well as Jews, and thinks the frivolous and unfounded stories of the Rabbies are meant, which their authors held to be important and wished to graft into the teaching of Christianity; he notes that Paul had been brought up amidst these superstitions and saw at once where they tended. Clarke says no people ever possessed a greater stock of them and points the reader to the Talmud. Ellicott gives the history behind the charge, that the Jewish schools taught an oral law delivered on Sinai and handed down by a succession of teachers, enlarged by the sayings of famous Rabbis, preserved for centuries by memory or in secret rolls and constantly receiving additions, a collection which contained some wise teaching along with much wild and improbable legend. On the genealogies Clarke understands the pedigrees that could never be made out in either direction, especially those bearing on the Messiah and the priesthood; Wesley distinguishes them from the genealogies of Scripture.

On the end of the commandment the question is what commandment is meant. Barnes reports that some take it for the gospel and others for the particular charge just given, and is anxious that Timothy should not be thought to hold the law of no consequence, since the teachers insisted much on its obligation and the remedy was correct views of its purpose rather than contempt of it. Gill takes it of the charge itself, whose design was to keep peace and brotherly love, both of which are hindered by speculative notions and genealogical contentions. Henry makes it the divine law and finds its whole scope in engaging us to love God and one another, so that whatever weakens either defeats the end of the commandment. Chrysostom turns the same word into a warning about friendship, that nothing is so injurious to mankind as to undervalue it, and that this is what has occasioned all heresies, since men who did not love their brethren came to envy those in high repute and from envy grew eager for power. Barnes insists that those who swerved never had what they missed, since a man who misses a mark need not first have hit it, while Ellicott reads the same verb as saying they had once been in the right direction and failed to keep in it.
8:
Both Gill and Barnes read the concession as a defence against an obvious charge. Having pressed so hard on men fond of being teachers of the law, Paul might easily be taken for an enemy of the law itself, and would be so represented by those he had just criticised; so he grants at once that the law is good, asking only that it be rightly understood and properly explained. Gill limits the concession to the moral law, since the ceremonial was by then annulled for its weakness and unprofitableness, leaving no lawful use of it at all. Wesley grants the whole Mosaic law instead, holding that even the ceremonial is good as it points to Christ while the moral is holy and just in its own nature, useful both to convince unbelievers and to guide believers. Clarke keeps a middle position, that the law as God gave it is good in itself and good in its tendency, and defines lawful use as interpreting it according to its own spirit and design; Ellicott sharpens that into a single function, that the law is used lawfully when it is used to make men conscious of sin and of deserving punishment.

The saying that the law is not made for a righteous man has been read in at least four ways, and Barnes lists them before choosing: some take the law here for the ceremonial code, some for the denunciatory part of it, and some hold that the chief purpose of law is simply to restrain the wicked. Clarke belongs to the third group and puts the case grammatically, that Paul does not say the law was not made for a righteous man but that it does not lie against him, since he does not transgress it, while it does lie against the wicked who have broken it and grievously. Wesley says the same in fewer words, that it does not strike or condemn him. Ellicott takes the righteous man to be the Christian in the full sense, justified by faith and sanctified, for whom the stern Mosaic code enacted centuries earlier was never framed. Gill guards the term itself, since no man is naturally righteous since Adam and none can be justified by the works of the law, so that the man meant is one made righteous by an imputed righteousness received by faith. Robertson notes the verb is the ordinary idiom for a law's being laid down.

Wesley finds an order in the catalogue of offenders that the others do not look for, matching the pairs against the commandments in sequence: the lawless and disobedient despise the authority of the lawgiver and so violate the first, which is the foundation of the law and the ground of all obedience; the ungodly and sinners break the second by worshipping idols or failing to worship the true God; the unholy and profane break the third by taking his name in vain. Robertson works the same list lexically instead, noting how many of its terms are rare or unique, several of them appearing nowhere else in the New Testament and one being a late form coined for the occasion. On the closing clause Gill gives the reason the gospel is invoked as the standard, that no doctrine is sound but what agrees with it, and piles up the titles the phrase carries: it is the gospel of God, of which he is the author and which relates to the glory of all his perfections, and it is the gospel of the blessed God, who is blessed in himself and the fountain of blessedness to others.
12:
Chrysostom takes the thanksgiving as a lesson in a rare virtue, remarking that the advantages of humility are generally acknowledged while the thing itself is nowhere to be found, there being affectation of humble talking enough and to spare; Paul cultivated it so far that he is always looking out for inducements to be humble, which men conscious of great merits must struggle to find, and he was the more exposed to the temptation because a good conscience swells a man like a gathering humour. Henry reads the verse for its doctrine of the ministry and gets three points from it: that putting men into the ministry is Christ's work, since ministers cannot properly make themselves and God condemned the prophets who ran unsent; that whom he calls he qualifies, so that men no way fit for the work were not of his putting into it; and that he gives not ability only but fidelity. Ellicott hears the pause behind the sentence, Paul stopping on the words about a gospel committed to his trust and overwhelmed by the flood of grateful memory that the thought let loose. Robertson notes the phrase for thanking is not used elsewhere by Paul.

Gill sets the thanksgiving against the men just described, who were fond of being teachers and called doctors of the law, whereas Paul counted it a high honour and special favour to be a preacher of the gospel and would not glory in gifts he had not given himself. Barnes finds the cost of it, that the call had required him to abandon his career of persecution together with every flattering scheme of ambition, and that if there is anything for which a good man should be thankful it is to have been so directed. Clarke reads the word for ministry at its plainest, as the deaconship or service of mankind by preaching, and takes the strengthening to include the miraculous gifts of the Spirit. On the confession that follows, Barnes is careful to say what the word blasphemer does not mean here, since Paul was not an open blasphemer in the modern sense, nor a profane swearer, his character having been the reverse and remarkable for treating sacred things with respect; what he had done was to revile the name of Christ and oppose his cause while not believing him the Messiah, and in that opposition he had really been guilty.

Ellicott will not soften the word as Barnes does, holding that Paul blasphemed in the truest sense of the terrible term, since a man who had seen Stephen die for Christ and afterwards did not cease to pant for the blood of the church must have known he was not merely reviling men but blaspheming God. Clarke sits between them, glossing the three terms as speaking impiously of Jesus, exterminating to the utmost of his power all who called on his name, and being as full of insolence as of malevolence, while thinking all the time that he did God service. What the plea of ignorance is worth then divides them further. Clarke takes it as the reason mercy was extended, Paul having acted under the prejudices that influenced his countrymen, while denying that it excuses the conduct. Wesley makes the same distinction the hinge of the verse and turns it against a doctrine: Paul does not say he obtained mercy because he was unconditionally elected, but because he did it in ignorance — not that ignorance took away the sin, but that it left him capable of mercy, which he would hardly have been had he acted against his own conviction.
15:
Ellicott identifies the opening formula as a fixed one, occurring only in the Pastoral Epistles and in a similar shape at the close of the Apocalypse, and takes such sayings for weighty and memorable truths well known and often repeated among the earliest Christians, rehearsed in their assemblies until they became watchwords in the churches scattered round the Mediterranean provinces, in which he sees perhaps the germs of the later creeds. Robertson adds that the phrase about Christ coming into the world is the language of the Fourth Gospel, which Paul could not have read, so that no formal quotation is in view but a knowledge of sayings already current among the disciples. Barnes treats the whole verse as something like a parenthesis thrown into the narrative because the writer's mind was full of the subject, having just said that he, a great sinner, had obtained mercy. Chrysostom explains why such a formula was needed at all: the favours of God so far exceed human hope that they are often not believed, and men receiving some great good ask themselves whether it is not a dream; what seemed incredible here was that enemies and sinners, justified neither by law nor by works, should be advanced through faith alone.

Clarke takes the two epithets in order and gives a reason for each: the saying is faithful because it may be credited without the slightest hesitation, God himself having spoken it and the death of Christ having confirmed it, and it is worthy of all acceptation because all men are sinners and justly condemned, so that what concerns every man deserves to be received by every man. Wesley says the same more briefly, that it is well deserving to be embraced with all the faculties of the whole soul, and presses the last word of the verse, that Christ came to save sinners without exception. Gill gives the formula a polemical edge, set as it is against fables, endless genealogies and contentions about the law, and unfolds what the faithfulness consists in: God's faithfulness to himself and to his own perfections, to his law which is thereby made honourable, to his word of promise now fulfilled, and Christ's faithfulness in carrying the work through. Robertson observes how many times the same formula recurs in these letters, and thinks that here a definite saying is being quoted rather than a sentiment merely expressed.

On the word chief Barnes corrects the English, since first here means not first in time but foremost in guilt, and explains the purpose: it was well to have one such example at the outset so that a doubt might never arise about the possibility of forgiving great transgressors, the question being thereby settled for ever. Robertson keeps both senses at once, the rank from the previous verse and the order of a man first in line, so that Paul becomes the specimen sinner; and he renders the word for pattern as a rough outline or sketch, a late and rare term. Ellicott draws the pastoral consequence, that Paul's conversion foretold much patient waiting on the Lord's part, a long-suffering that would not hurry to punish but tarry in hope of repentance, and Wesley reduces it to the shortest form, that none might hereafter despair. The doxology that follows is read by Robertson as a burst of gratitude and by Ellicott as a testimony to Paul's monotheism, addressed to no one Person but to a Godhead that is a sublime unity. Clarke construes King eternal as king of the eternity before time and the eternity after it.
18:
Chrysostom turns the mention of prophecies into a rule for choosing ministers, that the office of teacher and priest is of great dignity and to bring forward a worthy man requires a divine election, which is had when a choice is made without human passion, looking to no temporal consideration and swayed neither by friendship nor by enmity; he cites the apostles choosing Matthias before they had received the Spirit, committing the matter to prayer and looking to no human friendships, and complains that in his own day the church has advanced to the extreme of negligence. Henry reads the same verse as a definition of the ministry, a trust committed to men to see the gospel duly applied according to its Author's design, and takes up the military figure that follows: the ministry is a warfare, a good warfare against sin and Satan, waged under the banner of the Captain of our salvation. Robertson finds a different image in the opening verb, which properly means to set food beside a man and then to entrust, and is here a banking figure, so that the charge is a deposit lodged with Timothy for keeping.

What the prophecies were is less clear, and the answers differ in kind. Barnes takes them as hopes long entertained of the young man, so that in trusting him Paul acted in conformity with expectations already cherished about his usefulness. Clarke is careful to keep prediction and performance apart: the calling was foretold, but the behaviour in it was a matter of contingency depending on the use made of grace, which is exactly why the exhortation to war a good warfare is added. Wesley locates the occasion, that they were uttered when Timothy was received as an evangelist and probably by many persons. Ellicott reads the whole charge as a bequest, the last precious heritage which an old master, feeling the end not far off, would leave to his favourite disciple, and gathers its substance from what has just been said, that men should put their whole trust in him who came into the world to save sinners. Gill notes that the apostle has come back after a digression about his own conversion to the subject he began with, and that the charge includes preaching the gospel himself as well as forbidding others to teach otherwise.

Whether faith here means the doctrine or the disposition divides them. Gill and Clarke take it for the body of Christian truth, Gill making the holding of it a public holding forth in the ministry rather than a bare profession; Barnes reads it instead as fidelity, the loyalty a good soldier owes, which would include believing the truth but does not lead with it. The nautical figure that follows is worked hard. Clarke has the men thrust away conscience as a foolhardy soldier throws off shield and breastplate, or a mad sailor his pilot, helm and compass, and then suffer the wreck that follows; Robertson traces the verb to the word for a broken ship; Wesley keeps a different image, faith as a precious liquor and a good conscience as the clean glass that holds it. Wesley also presses the wreck to a conclusion the others avoid, that none can make shipwreck of faith who never had it, so that these men were once true believers and fell not only foully but finally, since ships once wrecked cannot afterwards be saved. Barnes and Gill identify Hymenaeus by his error about the resurrection and Alexander, probably, with the coppersmith.
